analysis.one_liner: Gives members of Congress real-time access to federal spending records, including payments to individuals and federal employees.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 4, 2025 with 17 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Oversight Committee; no vote or further action has occurred since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 so that members of Congress get a private, real-time feed of federal spending data through USASpending.gov — including the expanded detail that payments to individual recipients of federal assistance and to federal employees would count as covered 'entities' for that feed [S2]. The public website would stay as it is; the real-time, more granular version would be available only through a hyperlink accessible solely to members of Congress [S2]. The bill does not itself cut or add any spending; it is a data-access bill framed as making DOGE-style spending oversight a permanent congressional tool [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, members of Congress would gain a real-time window into federal awards and payments down to the individual level, which they could use to find waste, press agencies, or build cases for cutting programs, contracts, grants, or federal jobs. Agencies and programs already under spending scrutiny would face faster, more granular review.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress would get real-time access to updated federal award information through a dedicated link available only to them, instead of relying on the periodically updated public site [S2].

For that members-only feed, the bill expands the definition of 'entity' to include individual recipients of federal assistance and federal employees, so legislators could see payments made to specific people — data that is not exposed the same way to the general public under the current statute [S2].
The Office of Management and Budget would have to stand up the members-only link within six months of enactment, making the access operational rather than aspirational [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the main direct cost would fall on taxpayers as an administrative burden on OMB to build and maintain a real-time feed. Federal employees and individual recipients of federal assistance would bear an indirect cost: their individual payment records would become visible to 535 legislators, with no matching expansion of what the public can see, and the data could feed political campaigns to cut specific programs, grants, or jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal employees, grant recipients, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill is titled the 'Make DOGE Permanent Act' but contains no DOGE mechanism at all — no cuts, no commission, no sunset or extension of any executive cost-cutting body; its only operative provision is a members-only data link, so the title promises far more than the text delivers [S2].

The expanded information — payments to individual federal employees and individual recipients of federal assistance — would go to members of Congress only, not to the public, creating an asymmetry in which legislators get more detailed records about individuals than the people themselves or journalists can see on the public website [S2].

Individual-level payment data in the hands of every member of Congress creates a targeting risk: such records can be used to single out specific employees, grantees, or programs for political pressure or cuts, and the bill includes no restrictions on how members use the feed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Real-time spending transparency for legislators is a genuine oversight tool, and faster visibility into where money goes could help catch waste. But the bill's benefits are indirect and speculative, while the costs are concrete: an administrative build-out, an information imbalance that favors 535 officeholders over the public, and individual-level data on federal employees and grant recipients exposed to use in political targeting. The grand title does not match the narrow text, which suggests the bill functions more as a statement of support for DOGE-style cuts than as a working oversight reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 4, 2025 and referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, vote, or other action since [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Chip Roy introduced the bill in the House on June 4, 2025, joined by 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform [S1][S2][S4].
Seventeen House Republicans are listed as cosponsors; no Democrat has signed on [S3].
The action history shows no activity after the June 4, 2025 referral — no committee markup, no floor scheduling, no vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has yet — the bill has only been referred to committee, so the current spending-transparency status quo continues and no group has gained or lost anything.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat has signed on, and no vote has occurred to show how the chambers would divide.

industries.note: The bill would make individual federal employees' payment records visible to every member of Congress through a real-time feed, increasing exposure to politically driven job cuts and targeting, though the bill itself cuts no jobs [S2].

Their awards and payments would appear in real time to legislators, enabling faster scrutiny that could surface fraud but could also fuel pressure to cut specific grants and contracts; the bill changes no award terms [S2].

The bill's concrete beneficiary is the legislature itself: 535 officeholders would get a members-only, real-time, more granular spending feed than the public can access, expanding their information power over agencies and individuals without a matching public expansion [S2].
OMB would be required to build and maintain the members-only real-time link within six months of enactment, an administrative cost paid for out of existing agency resources [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With only 17 cosponsors, no Democratic support, and no committee action two months after referral, the bill is unlikely to move unless the Oversight Committee schedules a markup. Most private members' bills at this stage die quietly at the end of the Congress.
